Was skimming through subverses when I fell on this one, so I just wanted to give a bit of advice my mom always found helpful when trying to stay sober. She was an alcoholic and is sober now for around 30 years now.

Many people asked her how she did it for so long and she always responded by saying "I took it one day at a time"

Basically, instead of saying "I have to not drink/use/smoke forever" she would wake up each day and just tell herself "I have to not drink today." She said this helped because it wasn't so daunting when you take things one day at a time as opposed to thinking "I have the next 40 years of my life I have to not drink," etc.

It's also good to think about, at the end of each day, if you stayed clean, that you kept your promise that you made to yourself that morning.

Just give it a shot, if you're struggling with something, try just staying sober for today and keep doing that each day. Don't think about the future, just take it one day at a time.

I hope this advice helps someone out there. If not, that's okay.

Take it easy
Just something I learned from my alcoholic Mom.

I recall having these animated discussions with at least a couple of fellow recovering folks about how "we couldn't imagine never having a drink again" or "I might smoke pot again" or "I will want to have a glass of champagne at my daughter's wedding."

Looking back at those conversations now it seems rather silly I even spent any time obsessing over it - I definitely lacked a lot of perspective early on in my recovery. Right now? Who cares about whether I drink champagne or not at my daughter's wedding? If I toast her with a glass of Martinelli's or sparkling water, does it really matter? And why would I worry about something that is probably around 20+ years in the future, anyways?

Anyways, what got me through all that initial nonsense was the one-day-at-a-time stuff. Again, a lot of things I've picked up from 12-step are frequently pretty useful.

I've spent the last 2 years in Quebec, a French speaking province of Canada. I work from home dealing with Americans all day, and I've learned maybe 200 words of French while I've been here.

I'm embarrassingly mono-lingual, and I find learning this language incredibly painful and arbitrary. I tried DuoLingo for a while, and have moved on to Memrise which I find only slightly less painful.

So my questions is, have any of you discovered useful, fun methods for rapid language acquisition? Even finding a way to not actively and passionately hate the French language would be a huge win for me.

I would like to be a person that knows many languages, and I suspect a great many people feel that way.
I am mono-lingual myself but was going to reference this article when I get motivated / book a trip out of the country.

I started learning Spanish four months ago using the following:

I completed the doulingo Spanish tree, still do 10xp a day to keep my streak going

Anki, any SRS(read up on it) program will work, I like Anki. It is basically a digital flash are program that allows you to create a wide range of flash cards and carry them with you every on your mobile device. I added an entire phrasebook worth of material as well as FSI. I also add words I come across and don't know into Anki.

I have been using the FSI basic course(free) I read the lesson, add the phrases into Anki and listen to the lesson 4-5 times or until I am comfortable with the material.

I have stared reading books for young adults. The goal is not 100% comprehension. Instead I am trying to get as much exposure to different writing styles and sentence structures. It also really helps expand vocabulary.

I don't do as much listening practice as I should and it is my weakest point.

Practice speaking with as many people as possible. Find a Skype partner or someone local and talk frequently. Speaking will seriously be much harder than anything else since it usually the hardest to practice on your own. You can try to turn all of your internal dialogue into French. "I am hungry. I am going to eat this apple." If you don't know how to say apple, look it up and add it to Anki.

I have been doing this for 4 months now and I can have a 30 minute conversation in Spanish. I don't understand everything, my grammar is bad, my verbs aren't always the exact right conjugation, etc, BUT I can convey my message and understand what is being conveyed to me, mostly. Pretty rewarding honestly
